archiveRecords.title: Developing Digital Platforms to Help Older Adults Stay Physically and Socially Active: Co-Design Study to Develop a Toolkit and Evaluate Its Impact
archiveRecords.abstract: Digital technologies have the potential to support physical, cognitive, and social activity among older adults, but many small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) lack the resources to conduct meaningful co-design with older adults. Toolkits derived from rigorous co-design processes may offer a scalable mechanism for translating end-user priorities into real-world product development.  The Generating Older Active Lives Digitally study aimed primarily to engage older adults in a co-design process to identify priorities for digital technologies that support physical activity and reminiscence. Secondary  were to (1) translate these findings into a practical developer-facing toolkit, and (2) evaluate the toolkit’s perceived utility and influence among digital technology SMEs.  A total of 157 participants (121 older, 7 younger, and 29 staff) across 15 community and care settings in England and Scotland engaged in 106 technology interaction sessions, 22 evaluation focus groups, and 10 co-design workshops. These involved more than 20 digital technologies. Thematic analysis and structured card-ranking tasks were used to derive their priorities. Preliminary toolkits were co-designed and used by 10 UK-based SMEs who received small grants to apply the toolkit to active development projects. Their reports and follow-up interviews were analyzed thematically to identify perceived impacts on design decisions, product adaptations, and business outcomes.  Co-design activities generated 7 cross-cutting themes: motivation, content, barriers, design and inclusivity, suitability, acceptability, and motivations to use. These were organized into 3 toolkit sections: general design principles, online physical-activity platforms, and virtual reality. SMEs reported that the toolkits enhanced understanding of older adults’ needs, validated design decisions, and inspired some new features. Perceived impacts included improved usability, expanded accessibility options, increased content variety, clearer instructional design, enhanced social components, and reduced operational costs. SMEs also reported some business benefits, including strengthened cases for investment and increased product uptake.  Co-designed toolkits may offer a useful and cost-effective mechanism for translating older adults’ priorities into digital product development. SMEs perceived this toolkit as practical, relevant, and impactful for informing design choices. This approach may complement, but does not replace, direct user involvement. It may help accelerate inclusive digital-health innovation for aging populations.

archiveRecords.title: Gratitude and savoring interventions for older adults: a narrative review
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Gratitude and savoring have great potential to support well-being in older age, but most studies on positive psychology interventions have been conducted among healthy young adults. This narrative review explored gratitude and savoring interventions for older adults, with or without dementia, including (1) the characteristics of these interventions, (2) their acceptability for older users, and (3) their effect on mental health. Research Design and  Scopus, PubMed, PsychInfo, Web of Science, and CINAHL were searched in December 2023 and April 2025. Studies were eligible if they examined gratitude or savoring interventions among older adults. Multi-component intervention studies were excluded. Two researchers independently screened 2423 studies and assessed methodological quality using the Mixed  Appraisal Tool. Numerical and narrative data were extracted and synthesized regarding intervention characteristics, acceptability, and effectiveness.  Of the 11 included articles, five examined gratitude, five examined savoring, and one compared both. Only one study included participants with dementia. Adherence was generally high, suggesting a good fit, but participant evaluation was lacking. Four acceptability themes were highlighted concerning the target group, setting and delivery mode, dosage, and content and tailoring. Most studies showed improved well-being and reduced psychopathology, although not consistently on all outcome measures.  There is initial evidence that gratitude and savoring interventions could be suitable to promote mental health among older adults with relatively preserved cognitive function. Future research should examine the need for tailoring in terms of dose, delivery method and content, and applicability to more diverse groups of older adults.

archiveRecords.title: From ‘Old Man Yells at Cloud’ to Geronto-Futurism: Co-Imagining Holography and Aging
archiveRecords.abstract: This article explores the discursive, industrial, artistic, and practical interconnections between older people, aging, and holography, arguing that their nexus mutually shapes how both concepts are culturally constituted. Methodologically, the paper utilizes a discourse and representation analysis to examine a heterogeneous corpus of actual wave-optic holography and pseudo-holographic lens-optic phantasmagorias—collectively addressed as “(quasi-)holographic” phenomena. Dissolving the boundaries between cultural fiction and industrial technology, the analysis tracks two central thematic clusters revolving around exclusion and inclusion to interrogate how older adults are integrated into techno-social futures. The paper demonstrates that while older individuals are frequently subjected to exclusionary transhumanist logics or paternalistic, resource-scarcity-driven care practices, they also emerge as active agents of inclusive technology. By analyzing cases ranging from speculative science fiction to real-world care appliances, this study maps a neglected intersection in media and aging studies. Ultimately, it introduces the concept of “geronto-futurist” interventions. These practices not only expose the marginalized position of older adults in technological imaginations but actively reshape techno-futurities. By introducing an age lens to media practices, this article contributes to broader discussions of techno-social equality, highlighting how notions of later life actively shape contemporary understandings of digitality.

archiveRecords.title: Early life predictors of subjective cognitive function in older age: Emerging longitudinal associations over six decades
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Self-rated memory impairment is common in older age and has been related to  cognitive decline and dementia. Recently, there has been growing interest in early-life predictors of late-life cognition, but research has been limited due to the absence of data spanning the entire lifespan. The present study investigated whether psychological health, social well-being, socioeconomic status (SES), and cognitive abilities at age 10 and 13 predicted subjective memory almost six decades later.  Psychological health, social well-being, SES, and cognitive abilities were measured with standardized tests and questionnaires at age 10 and 13. Subjective memory, anxiety, and depressive symptoms were measured with the Prospective and Retrospective Memory Questionnaire (PRMQ) and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) at age 67 (n = 625).  In a longitudinal autoregressive structural equation model (SEM), higher levels of psychological health at age 13 predicted lower levels of subjective memory at age 67. This association was independent of current anxiety and depressive symptoms. The model did not provide sufficient support that social well-being, SES, cognitive ability, and school performance at age 13 predicted subjective memory at age 67. Additional analysis revealed that psychological health at age 13, but not at age 10, and anxiety symptoms at age 67 uniquely predicted subjective memory at age 67. Discussion These findings extend prior research by showing that psychological health is a robust predictor of subjective memory. Interventions targeting early-life psychological health may help identify individuals with different prospective cognitive outcomes in later life.

archiveRecords.title: Reproductive life course histories and menopausal outcomes at midlife: Evidence from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Menopause is a heterogeneous transition that varies in timing and type, yet population-based research rarely considers how reproductive life course experiences shape menopausal outcomes. This study examines whether reproductive timing, reproductive history, and reproductive health across adolescence and adulthood are associated with menopausal status, early menopause, and surgical menopause at midlife.  Using data from women in Waves I–VI of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), we constructed reproductive life course histories including pubertal timing, pregnancy and parity, reproductive complications, and gynecologic conditions. Menopausal outcomes at Wave VI included menopausal status, early menopause (before age 40), and surgical menopause. Survey-weighted logistic regression models estimated associations between reproductive characteristics and menopausal outcomes, adjusting for socioeconomic context and cumulative reproductive stress. Stratified analyses by pregnancy history assessed whether associations with gynecologic pathology were independent of fertility history.  At Wave VI (mean age 44), 18% of women were postmenopausal. Among them, 69% reported surgical menopause and 60% experienced menopause before age 40, indicating a substantial prevalence of non-natural and early transitions. Pregnancy and parity were consistently associated with menopausal outcomes, whereas reproductive timing showed more limited associations. Gynecologic pathology was strongly associated with early and surgical menopause independent of pregnancy history. Discussion Menopause emerges as a life course process shaped by reproductive histories and midlife reproductive health. The high prevalence of early and surgical menopause underscores the importance of examining heterogeneous pathways to menopausal timing and type in population-based research.

archiveRecords.title: Seeing no way out: Exploring the connection between internalized caregiver stigma, entrapment, suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms among Canadian informal caregivers
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Informal caregivers’ beliefs about caregiving for older adults (i.e. caregiver stigma) are associated with suicidal ideation and poor mental health. As only few studies have studied this association, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study analyzed whether caregiver stigma is associated with suicidal ideation and depression via feelings of entrapment.  Canadian long-term caregivers of adults aged 60+ years (N = 175, 18-95+ years) were surveyed online with the internalized caregiver stigma scale (self-devaluing (negative) and self-affirming (positive) stereotypes, attitudes, and behaviors), about their feelings of entrapment (short entrapment scale), depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation (PHQ-9). Regression analysis with robust standard errors and causal mediation analysis with bootstrapped standard errors were conducted.  Regression models indicated entrapment and negative care stigma were associated with more depressive symptoms, and entrapment with higher suicidal ideation. Significant indirect effects of positive and negative caregiver stigma components on suicidal ideation as well as depressive symptoms via entrapment were found in the causal mediation models. Additionally, positive caregiver stigma interacted with entrapment in the model for suicidal ideation. Discussion This study highlighted that the path from negative caregiver self-stigma to a higher level of suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms seems to be rooted through increased feelings of entrapment. Conversely, the self-affirming form of caregiver stigma had a hidden protective effect for both outcomes via lower feelings of entrapment. Targeting care-related stigma may thus help reduce the danger of negative mental health outcomes among caregivers of older adults by changing their constricting perception of being trapped.

archiveRecords.title: Outcomes Associated With Namaste Care for People With Dementia in Institutional Settings: A Systematic Review
archiveRecords.abstract: Namaste Care is a person-centered, non-pharmacological approach supporting comfort and engagement in institutional dementia care.  To synthesize quantitative evidence on clinical outcomes associated with Namaste Care among people with dementia living in institutional settings.  A systematic search was conducted across eight databases during February 2026. Quantitative studies evaluating Namaste Care or explicit adaptations were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the revised Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal checklists, and findings were synthesized narratively.  Thirteen studies were included, comprising 2 cluster-randomized controlled trials and 11 one-group pre-post studies. Favorable findings were reported for behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia, particularly agitation, although most came from uncontrolled studies. Some studies also reported reductions in pain or discomfort, whereas findings for quality of life were heterogeneous. Interpretation of findings was limited by uncontrolled designs, longitudinal attrition, and frequent discrepancies between planned and actual intervention doses.

archiveRecords.title: A Current Snapshot of Well-being Among Transgender Adults
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: Health challenges, including the onset, severity, and treatment of chronic health conditions, are differentially experienced by sexual and gender minority adults, resulting in health disparities. Using data from the 2023 CDC's BRFSS, we examine heterogeneity across age and transgender groups. American adults (N = 1282; M age = 32.38, SD = 14.5; 71.3% white non-Hispanic) provided data. We examine the number of poor mental health days (M = 13.7/30) and poor physical health days (M = 6.8/30) in the past month experienced by trans women (n = 404), trans men (n = 263), and trans diverse (n = 615) adults. Factorial analysis of variances examining poor mental health days revealed main effects for age and transgender groups, but no interaction between age and transgender identities. Similarly, main effects but no interaction emerged for poor physical health days.  are discussed in terms of the differential effects of environmental challenges on the health of transgender adults across the adult years.

archiveRecords.title: Enhancing Participation in an Undergraduate Aging Research Training Program
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: Research teams addressing inequalities in aging benefit from diverse perspectives that can strengthen the scientific rigor of the research. We developed a mentored research program to encourage diversity in population health aging research. Our program, Advancing Health Equity and Diversity (AHEaD), focused on reducing barriers to application and enrollment. We received robust interest in the program, including nearly 4,500 applications over 5 years (2021–2025), and welcomed 45 participants. Participants positively evaluated the application process. We received outcomes data on 40/45 participants as of September 2025, and 35/40 participants (87.5%) had engaged in research/employment, or were in the process of applying or had matriculated in graduate school. In summary, strategies designed to enhance participation and lower barriers to application yielded a high interest in our AHEaD program, and this interest was linked to high engagement in further research, employment, and education in population aging research.

archiveRecords.title: Reconstructing Identity in the Shadow of Dementia: Narrative Identity Processes Among Adult Child Caregivers
archiveRecords.abstract: Caring for a parent with dementia constitutes a profound relational and existential transition for adult children, extending beyond functional caregiving demands to processes of identity negotiation and reconstruction. Although extensive research has documented caregiver burden, psychological distress, and health consequences in dementia caregiving, comparatively little attention has been devoted to the narrative mechanisms through which caregivers sustain a coherent sense of self. Drawing on narrative identity theory, ambiguous loss theory, and the concept of biographical disruption, this qualitative narrative study explored how adult children construct identity narratives while caring for a parent with dementia. Semi-structured narrative interviews with 21 caregivers were analyzed using a holistic narrative approach informed by narrative selection theory. Four dominant narrative identity patterns emerged: management narratives emphasizing control and competence, growth narratives framing caregiving as personal transformation, protective boundary narratives focusing on identity differentiation, and fracture and alienation narratives. These narratives functioned as adaptive mechanisms for negotiating agencies, continuity, and moral positioning under conditions of chronic relational loss. The findings extend dementia caregiving research by conceptualizing caregiving as an ongoing narrative identity project rather than solely a burden experience, highlighting the central role of meaning-making, cultural expectations, and epistemic agency in caregiver adaptation.

archiveRecords.title: “You Don’t Belong in Hospital”: How Hospital-Based Dementia Stigma Shapes Health-Related Quality of Life
archiveRecords.abstract: Health-related quality of life reflects individuals’ perceptions of how a health condition affects their physical, psychological, and social functioning. Amid increasing pressures on primary care systems, people living with dementia are presenting more frequently to hospital settings. However, limited research has explored how hospital-based care, and the dementia stigma that may operate within it, shapes health-related quality of life for people living with dementia and their caregivers. This exploratory qualitative study involved semi-structured interviews with 15 participants, including people living with dementia and caregivers of individuals who had attended an emergency department or been hospitalized in Canada within the past two years. The interview guide was informed by the Wilson and Cleary Model of Health-related Quality of Life and intentionally avoided terms such as “stigma,” “bias,” or “discrimination” to reduce response priming. Data were analyzed using Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis and mapped to health-related quality of life factors (i.e., characteristics of the individual, biological and physiological factors, general health perceptions, etc.). Twelve caregivers (mean age 59.8 years, standard deviation = 9.7) and three people living with dementia (mean age 70.6 years, standard deviation = 11.8) participated between September and December 2025. Five interrelated discourses emerged: (1) characteristics of the individual: identity precedes clinical assessment; (2) biological and physiological factors: dementia disclosure as double-edged; (3) symptom and functional status: diagnostic overshadowing; (4) general health perceptions: equating dementia to futility; and (5) characteristics of the environment: structural barriers to recovery. Hospital-based discourses that implicitly or explicitly associate dementia with decline and therapeutic futility may contribute to stigma and negatively influence health-related quality of life for people living with dementia, while also intensifying caregiver distress. These findings underscore the need for stigma-reduction strategies in acute care settings that challenge therapeutic nihilism (i.e., inappropriately pessimistic view of patient outcomes) and promote person-centered, equitable hospital care.

archiveRecords.title: Termination of SNAP Emergency Allotments increased food insufficiency among older adults
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: We examined how the nationwide termination of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Emergency Allotments (EA) affected food insufficiency among older adults aged 60 and older, a group with high rates of nutrition-sensitive disease conditions and low SNAP uptake.  Using Household Pulse Survey data on older adult households with incomes below 200 percent of the federal poverty level, we applied a stacked difference-in-differences design to compare food insufficiency within three-month windows before and after EA termination.  Food insufficiency rose by 1.5 percentage points among older adult households overall and by 3.3 percentage points among older adults living alone, with no significant change among those not living alone. The difference in effects between those living alone and those not living alone was not statistically significant at conventional levels (p = 0.091). Sensitivity analyses restricting to self-identified SNAP recipients or varying the analytic window yielded consistent . Discussion These findings indicate that the loss of higher SNAP benefits substantially increased food hardship among low-income older adults post-COVID, underscoring the need for adequate benefit levels.

archiveRecords.title: Connected and Eager to Learn: Digital Skills, Challenges, and Unmet Needs of Older Adults in Long-Term Care Facilities
archiveRecords.abstract: This study explores the digital skills and challenges of older adults living in long-term care settings. We conducted 14 focus group interviews with 59 residents in Switzerland, with an average age of 80, to identify the competencies they possess and the skills they lack. Participants described using digital tools to stay connected and maintain autonomy. However, they also reported barriers such as cognitive limitations, rapid technological changes, and difficulty managing digital information. Despite these challenges, many expressed interest in improving their digital abilities. Our findings show that older adults in care settings want to engage with technology but often lack the necessary support. We conclude that providing hands-on training, simplifying digital interfaces, and offering ongoing assistance can reduce frustration, build confidence, and help residents manage daily tasks more independently.

archiveRecords.title: Building Student Skills and Belonging as Geroscience and Gerojustice Researchers Through a Longevity and Aging Research Education Program: A Qualitative Analysis
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: Addressing cumulative health disparities across the lifespan requires a scientific workforce trained at the intersection of geroscience and gerojustice. By integrating holistic academic and social support, an interdisciplinary Longevity and Aging minor, and scaffolded intramural and extramural research mentorship, the Katies for Aging Research and Equity (KARE) Program at St. Catherine University positions students to succeed as future aging researchers. To evaluate student growth, focus group transcripts, written reflections, Individual Development Plans, and student advocacy testimonials were examined. The qualitative analysis revealed three interconnected themes defining the scholar experience: (1) scholarly skill development, (2) belonging to a scholarly community, and (3) reframing longevity and aging. Beyond individual scholar growth, the KARE program has catalyzed broader institutional shifts, driving student-led research advocacy, interdisciplinary curriculum integration, and university-wide age-friendly initiatives. We offer a model for training future researchers to address complex health disparities in the intersecting fields of geroscience and gerojustice.

archiveRecords.title: Understanding Turnover Intention Among Institutional Eldercare Workers: A Structural Equation Model Based on the Conservation of Resources Theory
archiveRecords.abstract: This study aimed to examine the factors influencing turnover intention among institutional eldercare workers in China, drawing upon the Conservation of Resources (COR) theory.  China’s rapid population aging and increasing years lived with disability have substantially heightened the demand for long-term care services. However, workforce shortages and high turnover rates among eldercare workers remain critical challenges.  A cross-sectional survey involving 348 caregivers from 43 institutions in Zhejiang Province employed the Maslach Burnout Inventory, Caregiver Burden Scale, and Job Satisfaction Scale. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was utilized to assess direct, mediating, and moderating relationships.  Depersonalization, diminished personal accomplishment, and job satisfaction significantly predicted turnover intention. Job satisfaction fully mediated the relationship between occupational stress and turnover intention, while colleague support amplified the adverse impact of depersonalization.

archiveRecords.title: Factors Associated With Caregiving Burden and Psychological Distress Among Family and Unpaid Caregivers With Cardiovascular Conditions Caring for Older Adults
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examined factors associated with caregiving burden and psychological distress among informal caregivers with cardiovascular conditions (CVC). A secondary analysis of the 2024–2025 National Health and Aging Trends Study and National Study of Caregiving included 792 community-dwelling older adults and their caregivers with CVC. In the regression on caregiver burden, higher burden was linked to female gender, younger age, leg strength and low energy limitations, sleep disruptions, greater negative emotion, and longer caregiving hours, while higher positive emotion was protective. For psychological distress, higher distress was associated with caregiver breathing problems, difficulty returning to sleep, negative emotion, higher care support, and greater caregiving burden, whereas positive emotion was protective. These  indicate that psychosocial factors and physical challenges contribute to distress among caregivers with CVC. The association between care support and distress suggests support may be insufficient. Interventions targeting emotional well-being, sleep, and functional limitations may help reduce distress.

archiveRecords.title: Studying What Matters: South Texas Community-Driven Dementia Research Priorities
archiveRecords.abstract: South Texas has among the highest dementia prevalence rates in the United States, yet communities in the region remain consistently underrepresented in dementia research. Aligning research studies with what matters to communities most impacted by dementia is critical in addressing the crisis of research exclusion. This participatory study sought to identify community-driven dementia research priorities grounded in the experiences and needs of South Texas residents impacted by dementia. A two-year community-engaged study was conducted in partnership with a Community Council composed of individuals living with dementia, family caregivers, community health workers, and community-serving professionals. A plática program model was co-developed and implemented to elicit lived experiences with dementia and inform the development of a priority-setting survey. The resulting survey included 21 research topics grouped into four themes: (1) awareness of dementia, (2) experiences living with dementia, (3) families caring for someone living with dementia, and (4) resources to support families. Respondents ( N = 152) rated each topic on a 1–10 importance scale and selected their top two priorities by theme. Descriptive statistics were used to identify highly rated and frequently prioritized topics. Importance ratings were uniformly high across all topics (range: 8.44–9.39). Ranking data revealed clear priorities within themes wherein respondents prioritized timely diagnosis, improved provider communication, behavioral symptom management using non-pharmacological approaches, co-caregiving strategies, and system-level resources such as financial and legal planning supports. These priorities were largely consistent across respondent subgroups. The participatory approach of this study enhances the relevance of findings and demonstrates the value of community-engaged  for shaping research agendas. These community-defined priorities offer timely direction for researchers, funders, and policymakers aiming to reduce dementia disparities in South Texas and improve the equity, translational potential, and impact of future research.

archiveRecords.title: Napping Characteristics and Incident Dementia: Results From The National Health and Aging Trends Study
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Whether daytime napping may be a risk factor for dementia, in addition to nighttime sleep disturbances, remains unclear. This study investigated longitudinal associations of napping characteristics with incident dementia among U.S. older adults.  Data came from the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS). Napping characteristics were self-reported in a sleep module at round 3 (2013), including (1) frequency (non-napper, infrequent, frequent); (2) intention (non-napper, intentional, unintentional); (3) duration (non-napper, ≤30 minutes, >30 minutes). Dementia classification was established at each round using a validated algorithm and possible/probable dementia served as our outcome. We included 995 participants free of possible/probable dementia at round 3 who were followed up to round 13 (2023). Discrete-time complementary log-log models were used for hazard ratio (HR) of incident possible/probable dementia associated with napping characteristics, adjusting for demographic, health, and sleep variables (duration, daytime sleepiness, obstructive sleep apnea risk).  When compared to non-nappers, frequent nappers had 1.48 times the hazard of developing incident possible/probable dementia (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.14, 1.94). Unintentional napping was associated with incident possible/probable dementia (HR = 1.39, 95% CI: 1.06, 1.81). No associations were found for infrequent or intentional napping. Napping ≤30 minutes was associated with possible/probable dementia (HR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.06, 1.85), but the association of napping >30 minutes was attenuated with additional adjustment for sleep variables (HR = 1.28, 95% CI: 0.96, 1.69).  Daytime napping may be a modifiable risk factor for dementia if supported by further evidence. Future studies with detailed napping characteristics and longer follow-up are needed.

archiveRecords.title: Multidisciplinary prognostic accuracy in severe frailty: assessing short-term survival predictions in hospitalized older adults
archiveRecords.abstract: The increasing number of hospitalized older adults with severe frailty and limited life expectancy highlights the need for accurate short-term prognosis to inform care planning, effective communication, and resource allocation. However, survival prediction in this population is underexplored. This study aimed to assess (i) agreement among healthcare professionals on short-term prognosis, (ii) predictive accuracy of multiprofessional survival estimates, and (iii) factors affecting prognostic accuracy.  A prospective observational study was conducted on patients aged ≥ 65 years with severe frailty consecutively admitted to an Acute Geriatric Unit. All participants underwent Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment and screening for palliative care needs using the NECPAL tool. Healthcare professionals provided survival estimates at 1 and 3 months through a modified surprise question. Inter-rater agreement was assessed with Fleiss’ kappa. Kaplan-Meier curves were employed to compare survival across multiprofessional prognostic categories. The association between patient-related factors and prognostic accuracy was analyzed using logistic regression.  For the 117 patients included (mean age: 86.4 years, 57.3% female), prognostic agreement among healthcare professionals was moderate at both 1 month (κ = 0.475) and 3 months (κ = 0.528). Multiprofessional estimates classified 39.3% of patients as having an expected survival of 3 months. During the follow-up period, 47 patients (40.2%) died, 30% of whom tested negative for NECPAL screening. Estimates differentiated patients based on short-term survival (log-rank p  Reliable prognostic tools are needed to enhance care planning for severely frail older patients during the early stages of hospitalization. In this context, delirium assessment is crucial, as its presence significantly impacts the accuracy of short-term survival estimates, while the NECPAL tool demonstrated limited applicability.

archiveRecords.title: Internet Use and Digital Health Engagement Among Older Caregivers: Racial and U.S. South Regional Disparities
archiveRecords.abstract: Older Black informal caregivers in the U.S. South may face heightened healthcare challenges, yet digital technology may expand access to health resources.  This study examined racial and regional disparities in internet use and digital health engagement among older informal caregivers, focusing on Black caregivers in the South.  Data came from 900 Black and White caregivers aged ≥ 50 in the 2017–2020 Health Information National Trends Survey. Logistic regression models tested race-by-region interactions for general internet use and health-related online activities.  Black caregivers in the South had lower odds of general internet use and online communication with doctors, suggesting compounded racial and regional disadvantages. Among internet users, racial disparities in digital health engagement did not vary by region. Findings suggest that disparities may stem more from upstream barriers to digital access and general internet use. Addressing structural barriers to digital access is critical for advancing digital health equity.

archiveRecords.title: Understanding Dance Facilitation in Dementia Care: A Qualitative Study Using Socio-Ecological-Relational Framework
archiveRecords.abstract: Dance-based interventions are increasingly recognised as valuable psychosocial approaches to support the wellbeing and social participation of people living with dementia. However, existing research has largely focused on outcomes, with limited attention to how such programmes are facilitated and experienced in practice. This study explored how dance facilitators understand and navigate the multi-level influences shaping the organisation, delivery and perceived impact of dance sessions for people living with dementia and their informal caregivers. An exploratory descriptive qualitative design was adopted, using semi-structured interviews with six facilitators involved in a dance-based programme in Malta. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, guided by a socio-ecological–relational framework. Findings showed that dance facilitation is a relational and adaptive practice embedded within interacting individual, interpersonal, organisational, community and societal contexts. Facilitators continuously adjusted activities in response to participants’ cognitive, physical and emotional needs, using embodied and non-verbal approaches to support engagement. Relational processes, including shared movement and caregiver involvement, were central to fostering connection and inclusion. However, participation and sustainability were shaped by organisational environments, accessibility and persistent stigma, highlighting constraints beyond the control of facilitators. These findings emphasise that the value of dance lies in how it is enacted in practice, underscoring the need for supportive contexts.

archiveRecords.title: Atlantoaxial Instability in older adults: an underrecognized condition beyond rheumatoid arthritis – a retrospective study
archiveRecords.abstract: Atlantoaxial instability (AAI) is a well-recognized complication of rheumatoid arthritis (RA); however, its occurrence in elderly individuals without inflammatory rheumatic disease remains insufficiently investigated. Age-related degenerative and biomechanical changes may predispose geriatric patients to upper cervical instability independent of RA. This study aimed to evaluate the prevalence of radiographic atlantoaxial subluxation (AAS) in geriatric patients with and without RA and to assess whether radiographic AAS may be underrecognized in older adults without rheumatoid arthritis.  In this retrospective cross-sectional study, patients who underwent cervical computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging between January and September 2024 were evaluated. The study population included 206 patients aged ≥ 65 years with RA, 168 age-matched non-RA individuals, and 183 non-RA individuals younger than 65 years. Radiographic atlantodental interval measurements were obtained using standardized techniques, and AAS was defined as an interval exceeding 3 mm. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed with adjustment for sex.  Atlantoaxial subluxation was detected in 25.7% of geriatric RA patients, 12.5% of geriatric non-RA individuals, and 6.0% of younger non-RA individuals ( p  Radiographic atlantoaxial subluxation (AAS) was observed not only in patients with rheumatoid arthritis but also in older adults without RA undergoing advanced cervical imaging. These findings suggest that radiographic AAS may be more frequently observed among older adults undergoing advanced cervical imaging than is generally appreciated. However, the observed prevalence should not be interpreted as representative of the general geriatric population. Further prospective studies are warranted to determine the clinical significance of radiographic AAS and its implications for patient management.

archiveRecords.title: Correlates of Homebound Status by Rural/Urban Location, Socio-Demographic Characteristics, and Health Status
archiveRecords.abstract: This study seeks to identify factors that are associated with whether older adults are homebound in rural and urban areas. Utilizing the 2022/23 National Health and Aging Trends Study data, we conducted bivariate analyses to compare homebound status among rural and urban residents. Additionally, we used logistic regression to identify socio-demographic correlates overall and stratified by rurality and key demographic characteristics. The  revealed that rural and urban older adults had similar rates of homebound status, but that the association between risk factors and being homebound differed by rurality. In particular, older age, poor health, and Medicaid status were all more strongly associated with being homebound among rural older adults than among their urban peers. Varying socio-demographic factors are associated with the risk of older adults becoming homebound across rural and urban settings. Policies to prevent and support homebound older adults should be tailored to geographic and individual characteristics.

archiveRecords.title: Comparing sensor-based activity features of frailty across Fried Frailty Phenotype and deficit-accumulation frailty index
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Wearable sensors offer a low-burden approach to assessing frailty in free-living settings, but how sensor-derived features relate to different frailty definitions is unclear. This study compared thigh-worn sensor-derived activity features associated with pre-frail/frail status under the Fried Frailty Phenotype (FFP) and the Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment–Based Frailty Index (CGA-FI). Research Design and  We enrolled 44 older adults (mean age 82.3 years, 84% women) from senior housing communities. Participants wore a thigh-mounted ActivPAL accelerometer for 10 days and completed FFP and CGA-FI assessments. Thirty-four activity features were extracted across activity volume, postural transitions, gait, sedentary behavior, and diurnal variability domains. Point-biserial correlations compared feature associations with pre-frail/frail status under each frailty definition. Ridge, lasso, and random forest classifiers were evaluated secondarily.  Lower activity-volume features were associated with pre-frail/frail status under both definitions. Lower cadence was more strongly associated with FFP-defined pre-frail/frail status, whereas sedentary accumulation and lower inter-daily stability showed stronger associations with CGA-FI-defined pre-frail/frail status. Ridge logistic regression showed moderate discrimination of robust versus pre-frail/frail status (FFP: AUC 0.81 and F1 0.78; CGA-FI: AUC 0.79 and F1 0.77).  Thigh-worn accelerometry captured clinically plausible activity patterns associated with pre-frail/frail status under both definitions. Some individual feature associations differed in interpretable ways across definitions. Secondary analyses suggested that discriminatory information was largely overlapping in this sample. These findings support frailty-definition-aware interpretation of sensor-derived measures but do not imply the need for separate definition-specific multivariable models. Further evaluation of sensor-based frailty screening approaches is recommended.

archiveRecords.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences, Cognitive Outcomes, and Frailty in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are important life-course determinants of health and may contribute to vulnerability in later life. Frailty and cognitive outcomes are important concerns in older adults, yet evidence linking ACEs to these outcomes has not been systematically synthesized. This review evaluated the associations between ACEs and frailty or cognitive outcomes in middle-aged and older adults. Research Design and  Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched seven databases from inception to December 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed where possible, and remaining findings were synthesized narratively.  Twenty-six observational studies met the inclusion criteria. Five studies contributed to the meta-analysis of frailty outcomes and six to cognitive outcomes. ACEs were associated with higher odds of frailty (OR = 2.05, 95% CI 1.61–2.63),  cognitive impairment (OR = 1.46, 95% CI 1.18–1.82), and subjective cognitive decline (OR = 2.04, 95% CI 1.40–2.98). Narrative synthesis revealed substantial heterogeneity in the measurement of ACEs, frailty, and cognitive outcomes across studies.  ACEs are associated with increased risks of frailty and adverse cognitive outcomes in later life. These findings underscore the importance of a life-course perspective in aging research and suggest that childhood adversity may be relevant to later-life risk identification and prevention.

archiveRecords.title: Assessing concerns about falling: a comparison of telephone-based and face-to-face FES-I interviews in older adults
archiveRecords.abstract: Concerns about falling (CaF) are commonly assessed using the Falls Efficacy Scale-International (FES-I), but telephone versus face-to-face interviews may influence responses. The  of this secondary paired method-comparison analysis was to assess agreement between telephone and face-to-face FES-I total scores in older adults and to explore whether the two administration modes differed at the total-score and item levels.  Data were drawn from the FEARFALL study, a longitudinal randomized controlled trial on stress and functional health in older adults with CaF. FES-I scores of 123 participants aged 70 years and older were collected via both telephone and face-to-face interviews. Differences in total scores, item-level differences, and regression models were analyzed to identify potential influencing factors.  FES-I scores obtained during the telephone-first assessment were lower than those obtained at the subsequent face-to-face assessment ( p d = -0.34). Agreement between the two modes was moderate to good (ICC = 0.67). In addition, the two assessment modes showed a high correlation ( r = .71) with heterogeneity at the item level. Three items showed significant deviations (Item 4: “bathing/showering”, p adj = 0.007, d = 0.36; Item 10: “answer telephone”, p adj = 0.005, d = 0.34; Item 14: “uneven ground” p adj = 0.015, d = 0.32). Age was significantly associated with mode-related score differences ( B = -0.326, 95% CI [-0.58, -0.07], p = .013).  The telephone FES-I may be suitable for group-level comparisons and large-scale screenings. However, the interchangeability of telephone and face-to-face interview for individual clinical use remains uncertain. Since telephone assessment was always performed first and the time interval between assessments varied, the observed differences cannot be attributed to administration mode alone. Further studies specifically designed to compare administration modes are needed. Trial registration German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00029171), registered 22 July 2022.

archiveRecords.title: Reducing oral frailty improves functional independence in older Brazilians: A causal inference study of disability-free survival using longitudinal modified treatment policies
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Poor oral health is associated with functional decline and mortality in older adults, yet causal evidence linking oral health improvement with functional independence remains limited. We simulated the effects of hypothetical reductions in oral frailty on the cumulative probability of being alive and independent in basic activities of daily living (ADLs) among older adults in Brazil. Research Design and  Data from the EpiFloripa Aging Cohort Study of community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Florianópolis, Brazil, followed from 2009 to 2023, were analysed (1,702 participants). Oral frailty was measured at waves 1–3 using a seven-item composite score (range 0–7). The primary outcome was the cumulative probability of being alive and ADL-independent through wave 5, estimated using a discrete-time survival model. Longitudinal modified treatment policies with targeted maximum-likelihood estimation simulated nine oral health improvement scenarios, accounting for time-varying confounding and censoring.  336 deaths occurred during follow-up. A stepwise reduction in oral frailty increased the probability of being alive and ADL-independent by 73% (Probability Ratio 1.73, 95% CI 1.48–2.02), corresponding to 15,829 additional functionally independent older adults per 100,000 individuals. Preventing edentulism with preserved masticatory function also improved the probability of being alive and ADL-independent (Probability Ratio 1.21, 95% CI 1.08–1.36). Effects on survival alone were smaller and less certain.  Reducing oral frailty and preserving masticatory function increases functional independence among older adults, with smaller and uncertain effects on survival. Oral health is a modifiable determinant of healthy ageing.

archiveRecords.title: The National Archive of Computerized Data on Aging (NACDA) Portal: Variable-level discovery and custom metadata and data extraction for aging research
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Population aging has intensified demand for data infrastructure that supports life-course, cohort, and within-person research using longitudinal surveys. However, traditional file-centric dissemination and the growing number and diversity of aging data collections have complicated secondary analysis, limiting researchers’ ability to locate comparable measures, evaluate cross-wave continuity, and assemble cross-study analytic datasets. To address these challenges, we introduced the National Archive of Computerized Data on Aging (NACDA) Portal, a variable-level metadata discovery and extraction platform developed by NACDA in collaboration with Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research and Colectica. Research Design and  Established in 2019, the portal integrates 17 longitudinal aging studies encompassing over 210,000 variables. Organized by concept and harmonized metadata, users can identify and extract variables across waves and studies within standardized conceptual frameworks and generate tailored documentation to support transparent, reproducible workflows. We present a use case demonstrating metadata-driven, variable-level access for longitudinal data preparation and cross-study comparison.  The portal provides concept-oriented, variable-level discovery and extraction that streamlines identification of comparable measures, supports cross-wave assessment of measurement continuity, and reduces technical and cognitive burdens associated with assembling longitudinal analytic files. The use case illustrates how variable-level access and autogenerated documentation facilitate efficient dataset construction and reproducible analysis pipelines.  By shifting from file-centric dissemination to harmonized, concept-based metadata and variable-level extraction, the NACDA Portal lowers barriers to longitudinal and cross-study aging research. This approach can strengthen transparency, comparability, and reproducibility, supporting cumulative science as aging data resources continue to grow.

archiveRecords.title: Human Capital and Developmental Strengths: Older Adults and the Implementation of Age-Friendly Community Initiatives
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Discourse on age-friendly communities (AFCs) calls for the meaningful inclusion of older adults as partners and contributors to community-change processes. Nevertheless, there has been very little theoretical or empirical attention as to why older adults’ involvement matters. Our study aimed to address this gap by exploring the strengths-based qualities that older adults bring as implementation actors in AFC initiatives. Research Design and  We conducted a secondary analysis of qualitative interview data from 23 older adults across four states in the United States about their experiences leading or partnering on the implementation of AFC initiatives (e.g., as an AFC committee chair or workgroup member). We engaged in iterative rounds of coding and analytic memo writing using abductive qualitative analysis.  Three thematic categories emerged regarding qualities that older adults bring to AFC implementation processes: (a) accumulated knowledge of aging and the community (based on prior professional and life experiences, as well as long-time residency in the community), (b) continuity of specialized skills and abilities (such as volunteer management, integrative thinking, and entrepreneurial skills), and (c) values extension and congruence with the AFC initiative (valuing older adults and the community, as well as valuing the psychosocial opportunities of participation).  We situate our findings within the broader theoretical concepts of human capital and developmental strengths. We discuss how these theoretical orientations can promote the design of more optimal opportunities for older adults’ civic contributions through AFC initiatives, with strong potential to benefit individuals and communities alike.

archiveRecords.title: Cultural Contexts of Caregiving: Exploring Alzheimer’s Disease Experiences and Service Needs Among American Indian Communities
archiveRecords.abstract: and  American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN) experience disproportionately high rates of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD), yet little research examines caregiving experiences and service needs within these communities. Guided by the Sociocultural Stress and Coping Model, this study explored dementia caregiving experiences, cultural contexts, and service needs among American Indian community members, tribal health professionals, and leaders in a Northern Plains tribal community using a community-based participatory research approach. Research Design and  In 2024, seven focus groups were conducted with 60 American Indian adults (48 community members, 12 health professionals/tribal leaders) living in the Northern Plains. Semi-structured focus groups explored caregiving experiences, cultural beliefs, and service needs. A participant  survey captured demographics and care characteristics. Qualitative data were analyzed using conceptual content analysis with iterative team-based coding.  Three themes emerged across positive, negative, and service need domains. Community members emphasized cultural duty, love/reciprocity, and humor as coping mechanisms. Negative experiences included emotional and intergenerational trauma from childhood dementia exposure, and safety/supervision challenges. Critical service needs included medical guidance, community-based education, and respite services. Health professionals and tribal leaders navigated dual clinician-caregiver identities while advocating for system-level reforms. Both groups identified geographic barriers and resource scarcity.  Findings reveal cultural strengths sustaining caregiving amid substantial systemic barriers. Effective interventions must be family-centered, community-based, and strength-focused. Healthcare systems require fundamental realignment to accommodate Indigenous epistemologies.

archiveRecords.title: How shared-site intergenerational programs support psychosocial wellbeing in residential aged care: a realist evaluation
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Shared-site intergenerational programs, which co-locate services to enable interaction across generations, have gained attention for their potential to enhance psychosocial wellbeing in later life. However, evidence explaining how and under what conditions these programs are effective remains limited. This study examined how one of Australia’s few shared-site intergenerational programs supported older adults’ psychosocial wellbeing, staff experiences, and program sustainability. Research Design and  A realist evaluation was used to develop, test, and refine program theories explaining how contextual conditions interact with underlying mechanisms to generate outcomes. Data included realist interviews with residents, aged care staff, early childhood educators, and senior managers; organisational policy and procedure documents; and staff observation notes. Data were analysed using inductive, deductive, and retroductive reasoning to develop context-mechanism-outcome configurations.  Seven program theories were developed from twenty context–mechanism–outcome configurations. Psychosocial wellbeing was enhanced when intergenerational engagement occurred in safe and accessible environments, supported by skilled facilitation and organisational leadership, enabling participation to be experienced as meaningful and valued. These conditions activated mechanisms of belonging, reciprocity, and purpose, improving emotional wellbeing, social connection, and identity continuity. Staff experienced professional fulfilment and motivation when supported to facilitate quality engagement, while strong organisational culture contributed to sustainability. Outcomes varied where contextual supports were constrained.  Shared-site intergenerational programs function as complex relational and organisational interventions. Psychosocial benefits for residents, alongside staff wellbeing and program sustainability, depend on alignment between facilitation practices, organisational culture, and everyday institutional conditions.

archiveRecords.title: The Weight of Care: Examining the Relationship Between Grandchild Caregiving and Adiposity in Later Life
archiveRecords.abstract: Grandchild caregiving is an increasingly common later-life family role, yet its association with older adults’ adiposity remains unclear. Using five waves of the Health and Retirement Study (2010–2018), this study examines associations between grandchild caregiving arrangements and four adiposity indicators: BMI based on self-reported height and weight, physically measured BMI, waist circumference, and relative fat mass. Linear panel models, including random-effects and fixed-effects models, assess whether adiposity patterns are linked to caregiving transitions or to broader differences across caregiving arrangements. Fixed-effects  showed little evidence linking caregiving transitions to adiposity changes over time. Random-effects models indicated higher adiposity among grandparents in household caregiving arrangements, especially multigenerational households, across multiple outcomes. Findings suggest that later-life adiposity differences among caregiving grandparents are linked less to caregiving transitions per se than to the household, socioeconomic, and family-role contexts in which grandchild care occurs.

archiveRecords.title: How aging shapes interoception: A multimodal, multidimensional analysis
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Aging is known to influence perceptual sensitivity, yet its effects on interoception across the lifespan remain poorly understood. Prior research has largely focused on single interoceptive dimensions (e.g., interoceptive sensitivity) or modalities (e.g., cardiac interoception). Moreover, most studies have assessed interoception at rest, limiting insight into how individuals track real-time changes in interoceptive state. In this study, we examined age-related differences in both interoceptive sensitivity and sensibility across cardiac and respiratory modalities in healthy adults.  In a single session, participants (N = 78; aged 18-79 years; M age = 49.10) were assessed for: 1) interoceptive sensibility using the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (Version 2); 2) cardiac interoceptive awareness using a heartbeat tapping task under baseline and breath-holding perturbations; and 3) respiratory interoceptive awareness using an inspiratory load estimation task with varying resistance levels. Using the non-invasive interoceptive perturbations, we elicited dynamic fluctuations in interoceptive signals. Associations between age-related differences in interoceptive awareness measures were examined using linear mixed-effects models.  Our  revealed that older age was associated with reduced cardiac interoceptive sensitivity during breath-holding, while respiratory sensitivity remained stable across ages. Additionally, interoceptive sensibility increased with age, suggesting that task-based interoceptive performance and self-reported sensibility may follow divergent aging pathways. Discussion These findings demonstrate that interoceptive awareness does not decline uniformly with age but instead varies by modality and dimension. By identifying how aging differentially impacts interoceptive sensitivity and sensibility across systems, this study opens new avenues for characterizing age-related changes in interoceptive awareness and bodily regulation.

archiveRecords.title: The Respective Roles of Negative and Positive Views of Aging in Predicting Rehabilitation Outcomes
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Subjective views of aging (VoA) predict health outcomes, yet most studies rely on specific measures of VoA in relatively healthy samples. Referring to multidimensional (generalized and personal) and multidirectional (negative and positive) VoA constructs, we examined whether these VoA differentially predict rehabilitation outcomes among older adult patients coping with hip fracture and stroke.  One hundred and fifty-eight geriatric rehabilitation patients (mean age=77.15, SD=6.71) reported VoA at admission while referring to negative and positive generalized (Attitudes to Aging Questionnaire, AAQ) and personal views (awareness of age-related changes, AARC). Patients' functional independence was evaluated by healthcare personnel at admission and discharge, and rehabilitation efficiency (RE) was computed to reflect functional improvement relative to potential. Path analyses tested the unique contributions of negative and positive VoA (for both generalized and personal views) while adjusting for other predictors of RE.  For both generalized and personal VoA, negative views (i.e., AAQ-Losses and AARC-Losses) predicted lower RE, whereas positive views (i.e., AAQ-growth and AARC-Gains) did not show significant effects on RE. Negative views had a significantly stronger effect on RE than positive views, but only for the AAQ subscales. Discussion In the rehabilitation context, negative VoA, referring to age-related losses, appear more consequential for functional recovery than positive VoA (referring to age-related growth and gains). Findings support prioritizing interventions that identify and modify both generalized and personal attitudes, especially those focused on age-related losses, during rehabilitation to enhance functional outcomes.

archiveRecords.title: Past-Month Tobacco and Cannabis Co-Use by Chronic Disease and Sociodemographic Factors Among U.S. Adults 65+ Years (2021-2023)
archiveRecords.abstract: Tobacco and cannabis co-use prevalence is rising, with older adults disproportionately impacted.  Assess tobacco and cannabis co-use by health and sociodemographic characteristics among adults 65+ years.  Using National Survey on Drug Use and Health nationally representative data (2021-2023), we estimated past-month tobacco and cannabis co-use prevalence among adults 65+ years ( N = 15,672). Multinomial logistic regressions examined associations between health and sociodemographic characteristics with past-month co-use, tobacco-only use, and cannabis-only use (vs. former use).  One in six reported past-month use of either cannabis or tobacco (1.7% co-used). More chronic disease diagnoses was associated with lower co-use (e.g., one vs. none: adjusted relative risk ratio [aRRR] = 0.47). Co-use was higher among people with worse self-rated health (e.g., fair/poor vs. excellent/very good: aRRR = 2.73) and past-year mental illness (aRRR = 2.07).  Clinicians working with older adults should account for cannabis co-use in tobacco cessation and disseminate evidence-based cannabis information.

archiveRecords.title: Advancing the Evidence Base for Adult Day Services: A New Five-Year Research Agenda for 2026–2031
archiveRecords.abstract: Adult day services (ADS) provide care and social support for adults with complex health needs, yet they remain an understudied long-term care sector whose impact on patient outcomes is unclear.  To inform an updated research agenda that supports a coordinated approach to measuring impact of ADS and gaps in services in an evolving policy landscape.  We convened 32 stakeholders in partnership with the National Adult Day Services Association. Following a pre-convening evidence review, a facilitated discussion took place. Rapid qualitative synthesis of notes was used to identify themes and consensus priorities.  Participants’ priority was strengthening data infrastructure. They wished to leverage data to identify workforce shortages, implement evidence-based interventions, advance policymaker understanding of ADS, and address uneven reimbursements. The agenda prioritizes standardizing outcome measures, supporting workforce capacity, and translating research into policy. These stakeholder-informed priorities can guide research and policy to demonstrate impact and expand access to ADS.

archiveRecords.title: From ‘a Normal Part of Aging’ to ‘an Explanation for my Symptoms’: Insights From Patient-Care Partner Dyad Interviews About the Cognitive Impairment Diagnosis Process in Primary Care
archiveRecords.abstract: Despite increasing pressure on primary care clinicians to provide accurate and timely assessment and diagnosis of cognitive impairment (CI), many remain unprepared. To inform improvement, we conducted interviews with 20 dyads of recently diagnosed patients and their care partners (spouses or adult children) to better understand experiences with CI assessment and diagnosis in primary care. Dyads reported wide variation in how primary care responded to their initial cognitive concerns, ranging from compassionate prioritization to minimization or attribution to age and/or physical comorbidities. Dyads also reported variability in testing, time to diagnosis, and the CI diagnosis experience. Many dyads described the challenges of living with CI including stigma, loneliness, and a desire for more support from primary care clinicians.  identify specific areas of potential improvement in the primary care of individuals with cognitive concerns that should be embedded into point-of-care clinical decision support tools for primary care.

archiveRecords.title: A generalized approach for estimating the pace of aging
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Quantifying the rate of aging is essential for understanding age-related physiological decline and predicting late-life outcomes. The Pace of Aging (PoA) framework addresses this by modeling longitudinal changes across multiple biomarkers. However, the original Dunedin PoA assigns equal weight to all biomarkers and was derived from a young cohort with limited mortality follow-up, which restricts its applicability in older populations and in settings where biomarker relevance is uncertain.  We developed a weighted Pace of Aging (wPoA) using data from the Swedish Adoption/Twin Study of Aging (SATSA), a longitudinal cohort of older adults with up to nine waves of biomarker data collected over three decades. Using mixed effects models, we estimated individual random intercepts and slopes for 10 biomarkers and assigned weights to these random effects based on their association with time-to-mortality. This mortality-informed weighting distinguishes the wPoA from the original Dunedin PoA.  We found that wPoA was positively correlated with established biological age predictors and more strongly correlated with low-dimensional predictors such as Functional Aging Index (FAA) and the Frailty Index (FI). Modest correlations across all considered predictors suggest that each measure captures distinct aspects of biological aging.  In , the wPoA framework introduces a data-driven weighting of random effects and is particularly well-suited for aging cohorts and in settings where marker relevance is uncertain a priori, such as high-dimensional or omics-based contexts. This work provides a foundation for future single-timepoint surrogates that can also be used in settings lacking rich longitudinal data.

archiveRecords.title: Effect of an Intersectoral Telemedicine Intervention on Hospitalization in Nursing Home Patients: Specification Curve Analysis of a Stepped Wedge Cluster Randomized Trial
archiveRecords.abstract: The use of emergency medical services in Germany has significantly increased, particularly for nonemergency cases. This issue becomes especially relevant for nursing homes, where staff is confronted with resource shortages and organizational challenges, making emergency medical services involvement a common course of action. This leads to potentially avoidable hospitalizations for nursing home residents and exposes them to severe health risks, such as nosocomial infections. To address this, we developed the Optimal@NRW project, implementing an innovative intersectoral telemedicine intervention that includes an early warning system and mobile nonphysician medical assistants in order to enable outpatient treatment in acute medical cases for nursing home residents. We hypothesize that hospitalizations could be significantly reduced, as patients could be treated on-site in the absence of a life-threatening emergency.  This study aims to determine the effect of an intersectoral telemedicine-based intervention for acute care situations on hospitalization among residents in nursing homes.  We conducted a prospective multicenter cluster-randomized stepped wedge trial from May 2021 to April 2023 across 24 nursing homes in western Germany. Nursing homes were randomly assigned to one of four sequences and followed over eight 3-month periods. All sequences crossed stepwise from the control to the intervention phase. We collected primary data in an electronic patient record and claims data from statutory health insurance funds. In a specification curve analysis, we evaluated the intervention effect using multiple mixed-effects regression model specifications with varying modeling approaches, datasets, dependent and independent variables, and operationalizations.  The number of participants ranged from 158 to 285 nursing home residents per sequence and period, totaling 1151 participants in the control phase and 1271 participants in the intervention phase. A total of 1260 regression models were analyzed. Approximately two-thirds of all models exhibited a negative (ie, protective) intervention effect. However, no models exhibited a statistically significant (ie, P  Our  do not support the hypothesis of a significant reduction of hospitalizations among nursing home residents. The effectiveness of the intervention may have been compromised by external factors such as a flood disaster in the study region and the COVID-19 pandemic, which introduced unforeseen challenges. Future studies should prioritize targeted outcomes (potentially avoidable hospitalizations) that align with the specific intervention mechanism, while also allowing for extended implementation periods to ensure that interventions reach their full potential.

archiveRecords.title: Experiences of Family Caregivers Supporting Older Adults With Limited English Proficiency in Accessing Preventive Healthcare: A Qualitative Interpretive Study
archiveRecords.abstract: This study explored how immigrant family caregivers support older immigrant adults with limited English proficiency (LEP) in using primary and preventive care and how these roles shape caregivers’ lives. A qualitative phenomenological study was conducted with 32 immigrant family caregivers of older adults with LEP in the United States, purposively recruited from prior LEP-focused studies. Participants completed one interview, and data were analyzed using an interpretative phenomenological, descriptive thematic approach. Caregivers described extensive, often invisible work as decisionmakers, system navigators, interpreters, cultural brokers, and emotional and transportation support, frequently conflicting with employment and family obligations and contributing to strain, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and ambivalence about parents’ migration. Repeated communication problems and perceived disrespect fostered mistrust of healthcare institutions, shaping preventive care engagement. Immigrant family caregivers act as pivotal intermediaries who compensate for structural language and access barriers, underscoring the need for language-concordant, culturally responsive, caregiver-inclusive services and stronger work–care supports.

archiveRecords.title: Effect of Watch–Assess–Need Intervention–Think Model Education and Training Program for Family Caregivers in Dementia Care
archiveRecords.abstract: Most family caregivers of people living with dementia in Taiwan only receive initial dementia-related information after diagnosis, with limited subsequent training in dementia care management, which may contribute to caregiver stress. The purpose of this study is to test the effectiveness of the Watch–Assess–Need Intervention–Think (WANT) model education and training program in enhancing family caregivers’ dementia care competence and self-efficacy. A pre-post experimental design was conducted with a mixed- approach for data collection. Ninety family caregivers of people living with dementia recruited from the communities were randomly assigned to an experimental group and a control group. The experimental group received the WANT program for one month, while the control group maintained their usual lifestyle. This study utilized a demographic questionnaire, a dementia care competence scale, and a dementia care self-efficacy scale to collect pre- and post-test data. Additionally, qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews.  showed that dementia care competence, knowledge, skills, and self-efficacy of the experimental group significantly improved; however, the program led to only a minor change in attitude. There was no significant difference across variables for the control group. The qualitative interviews generated three themes: (1) acquiring knowledge and caregiving skills to effectively respond behavioral expressions; (2) acquiring self-adjustment  to improve relationships with family members with dementia; (3) changing attitudes to learn to care for and empathize with family members of people living with dementia. Overall, the WANT program effectively enhanced participants’ knowledge, skills, and self-efficacy. Participants developed self-regulation strategies, improved their relationships with family members living with dementia, and strengthened their ability to understand and respond to behavioral expressions. The WANT program can be applied in future to support family caregivers in providing person-centered responses to behavioral expressions and improving caregiving outcomes.

archiveRecords.title: Social, economic, and environmental disparities in device-measured 24-hour movement behaviours in a nationally representative cohort of older English adults
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Insufficient physical activity, excessive sedentary time, and suboptimal sleep duration (i.e., not excessively short or long) are linked to morbidity and premature mortality and may contribute to health inequalities, but device-measured, nationally representative data capturing the full 24-hour movement spectrum remain scarce, particularly among older adults. This study examined social, economic, and environmental disparities in 24-hour movement behaviours in the 2021-23 English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) accelerometry sub-study.  A subset of 5,382 ELSA participants (71.9%) was invited to wear a wrist accelerometer for eight days, with 4,354 (80.9%) agreeing. Raw data were processed using three distinct machine learning algorithms to estimate step count, sleep duration, moderate-to-vigorous and light physical activity, and sedentary time. Cross-sectional associations with sex, age, education, marital status, wealth, and urbanicity were examined using linear regression.  Data from 3,648 participants (mean age 68.5 ± 9.3 years; 44.3% male) were included in the wear time analyses (median 6.6 days, IQR 6.0-6.9) and data from 3,161 (86.7%) participants with sufficient wear time were included in the 24-hour movement behaviour analyses. Older, unmarried, or lower education/wealth participants were less active, more sedentary, and slept less. Rural participants were more active than urban participants. Females accumulated fewer steps and less moderate-to-vigorous activity and sedentary time, but more light activity and longer sleep than males.  Social, economic, and environmental disparities exist across the full 24-hour movement spectrum, highlighting groups for targeted interventions. Follow-up will clarify how 24-hour movement behaviours influence healthy ageing and contribute to health inequalities.

archiveRecords.title: Exploring the Shared Genetic Architecture of Sarcopenia Using Genomic Structural Equation Modeling
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Sarcopenia is a common age-associated condition characterized by the progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical functionality. While large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have previously addressed isolated traits of sarcopenia, the multifactorial genetic architecture underlying this condition remains largely undefined.  To characterize the common genetic basis of sarcopenia-related traits, genomic structural equation modeling (Genomic-SEM) was implemented. Multiple post-GWAS analytic approaches were integrated to pinpoint susceptibility loci. These analyses encompassed identifying enriched genetic pathways and relevant genomic elements, as well as cell-type-specific enrichment in skeletal muscle satellite stem cells, mesenchymal stem cells, and skeletal muscle satellite cells in limb muscle. Furthermore, based on the integrated GWAS data of sarcopenia-related traits, polygenic risk score (PRS) analysis was conducted to evaluate risk associations at the chromosomal level.  A well-fitted Genomic-SEM successfully integrated the GWAS data, revealing the shared genetic architecture of sarcopenia-related traits. We identified 110 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) reaching genome-wide significance (P  This study provides a comprehensive genetic characterization of sarcopenia via Genomic-SEM, offering new insights into the etiological pathways underlying sarcopenia.

archiveRecords.title: construction and evaluation of sarcopenia risk prediction model for non-obese older adults
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction: Sarcopenia is common in older adults, with distinct features in non-obese individuals. This study developed and validated a nomogram to predict sarcopenia risk specifically in non-obese older adults. : Data from 1,654 CHARLS participants were used for model development and internal validation, and 263 NHANES participants for external validation. LASSO regression selected predictors. A nomogram was constructed and assessed using AUC (discrimination), calibration curves (accuracy), and decision curve analysis (clinical utility). : Seven variables were included in the final nomogram: age, sex, BMI, hemoglobin (Hb), difficulty rising from a chair, history of falls, and basic living ability. The model demonstrated excellent discrimination, with an AUC of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.86-0.90) in the training set. Performance remained robust in the internal (AUC 0.89, 95% CI: 0.85-0.92) and external (AUC 0.94, 95% CI: 0.91-0.97) validation sets. In the sex-stratified analysis, age, BMI, BUN, liver diseases, and basic living ability were included in the male model (AUC: 0.95, 95% CI: 0.93-0.97). For females, age, BMI, creatinine (Cr), difficulty running 1 km, and basic living ability were included (AUC: 0.83, 95% CI: 0.79-0.87). All models demonstrated good calibration and clinical utility. : This study established an effective and simple prediction model for sarcopenia in non-obese older adults. This nomogram can serve as a valuable clinical tool for the early identification and proactive management of sarcopenia in this specific population.
